planting.note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 8b–9 the top growth is often killed by hard freezes but the plant regrows from the base once the ground warms.

directions: Plant in well-drained, gritty to loamy soil in full sun to light partial shade, where clusters of narrow, tubular scarlet-red flowers open at the branch tips from summer into fall. Scarlet bouvardia is a wiry, open subshrub native to the dry mountains and canyons of the southwestern United States and Mexico, and its bright, nectar-rich flowers make it a dependable hummingbird plant for the second half of the growing season, when many spring bloomers have finished. It is naturally drought tolerant and resents heavy, poorly drained soil far more than it minds dry spells, so plant it on a slope or in a raised bed if native soil is slow to drain. Cut plants back hard in late winter to remove any freeze-damaged wood and to keep the naturally leggy growth habit dense and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; protect from afternoon sun in zone 8–9 to keep the gold leaf center from bleaching or scorching.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Orange Marmalade produces broadly heart-shaped leaves with a bright gold to chartreuse center that deepens toward orange-gold tones as the season progresses, set off by a narrow, irregular dark green margin. It forms a tidy, mounded clump of medium size, making it useful as a specimen or grouped along a shaded bed edge where its warm coloring stands out against the more common blue and green hosta tones. Pale lavender flowers rise on scapes above the foliage in mid to late summer. Divide congested clumps in early spring as new growth emerges, and mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool through hot Gulf South summers.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; consistent moisture keeps the deeply cupped leaves from flattening out in Gulf South heat.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this award-winning cultivar produces exceptionally thick, heavily corrugated blue-green leaves that cup so deeply they will genuinely hold a puddle of water or a scoop of birdseed after a rain, a distinctive trait its name describes literally. The dense, mounded clump has excellent substance and slug resistance for a blue hosta, since blue-leaved cultivars are often thinner-leaved and more vulnerable. Near-white flowers appear on stout scapes in early to midsummer, held mostly within or just above the foliage. Divide in early spring only when necessary, since this cultivar is slow to reach full size and resents frequent disturbance; established clumps make an outstanding textural anchor for a shaded border.

common_name: Rainbow's End Hosta (Miniature Gold-Centered White-Margined Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; site along a bed edge or in a trough where its small scale won't be lost among larger companions.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Rainbow's End is a miniature hosta with small, pointed, creamy white-margined leaves centered in bright gold that brighten as the season progresses, forming a tight, tidy mound well suited to rock gardens, container plantings, and the front edge of a shaded bed. Pale lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer, in proportion with the compact foliage. Because miniature hostas have shallow root systems, keep the soil consistently moist and mulched, especially through Gulf South summer heat, and avoid planting where competing tree roots will out-compete it for water. Division is rarely needed and best done sparingly in early spring, since miniature hostas take a few seasons to bulk up to a dividable size.

common_name: Full Eclipse Louisiana Iris (Near-Black Award-Winning Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer or fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Full Eclipse is a modern award-winning Louisiana iris cultivar bred for exceptionally deep, near-black purple flowers that read as solid dark velvet even in strong light, a striking contrast when paired with the paler blues, whites, and yellows more typical of the class. As with other Louisiana iris, consistent moisture is the key to strong bloom, so it performs best at a pond edge, in a rain garden, or in a low spot that other perennials find too wet. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer, replanting fans promptly since exposed rhizomes dry out and lose vigor quickly.
